title: Brazil's Presidential Election Heads to a Run-Off
summary:
Brazil's presidential election will be decided in a second round of voting on October 25. In the first round on Sunday, no candidate won more than 50 percent of the votes, which is what is needed to win outright.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a right-wing politician, finished first. He beat Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the left-wing president who is now in office. Bolsonaro's result was better than many people expected. He is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for leading a failed coup attempt after losing the last election. Jair Bolsonaro was not allowed to run again, so he backed his son.

Lula is 80 years old and is asking voters for a fourth term. He was first elected in 2002 and again in 2006, and he won a later term in 2022. After voting, he said the choice was between democracy and "barbarism." Bolsonaro, who is 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people."

The campaign has divided the country again. Voters said top concerns included the economy, crime, corruption and Brazil's independence from other countries. Lula is more popular in the poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics and women. Bolsonaro is more popular in the south and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.

During the campaign, Lula accused the United States of trying to influence Brazil's election. On Sunday, the head of Brazil's top electoral court said no evidence of international interference was found.

Brazil is the largest country and economy in Latin America. Most countries in the region now have right-wing leaders, so the run-off will help show whether Brazil follows that pattern.
why_it_matters: The result will help decide who leads Latin America's largest country and shows how voters there feel about the economy, crime and corruption.
